Overview of the Nervous System
Aftab Merchant, MBBS, FCPS, MHPE
Professor of Medical Education
Assistant Dean of Anatomical Education
Kirk Kerkorian School of Medicine
University of Nevada Las Vegas

Learning Objectives (2026)
1. Describe the structural and functional organization of the nervous system, including the
CNS, PNS, sensory pathways, motor pathways, and autonomic divisions. (CLO 1, CLO 2)
2. Apply standard neuroanatomical terminology to describe orientation, sections, gray matter,
white matter, nuclei, tracts, nerves, and ganglia. (CLO 1, CLO 5)
3. Relate the structural organization of neurons, glial cells, and major neural pathways to
normal nervous system function and the principles of neurological localization. (CLO 1, CLO
2, CLO 5)
Pre-Session Assignment
• Preview the PowerPoint slides. You are not expected to memorize details before class.
• Watch: B&B: Cells of the Nervous System (23 min)

Structural Division – Where Structures Are Located
Central Nervous System (CNS)
• Brain
• Spinal cord
Peripheral Nervous System (PNS)
• Cranial nerves
• Spinal nerves
• Peripheral nerves
• Ganglia
Fig. 1.5 Central and Peripheral Nervous System.
Crossman, Neuroanatomy, 6e.

Functional Organization of the Nervous System
Nervous System
SENSORY (Afferent) MOTOR (Efferent)
Peripheral receptors → CNS CNS → Effectors
Somatic Motor Autonomic Motor
(Voluntary; skeletal muscle) (Involuntary; smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, glands)
Sympathetic Parasympathetic
(Fight or Flight) (Rest and Digest)
Structural divisions tell us where neural structures are located.
Functional divisions describe the direction and function of neural pathways.

Spinal Nerve
Anterior Root
• Carries motor (efferent) fibers
• Somatic motor: cell bodies in anterior horn
• Autonomic motor: preganglionic neuron cell bodies in
intermediate gray matter
Posterior Root
• Carries sensory (afferent) fibers
• Sensory neuron cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion
• Anterior + posterior roots unite → mixed spinal nerve
• Spinal nerve exits via intervertebral foramen
• Divides into mixed anterior and posterior rami
Fig. 2.9 Spinal nerves (transverse section).
Anatomy for Students, 5e.

Autonomic Nervous System
Autonomic motor pathways
regulate:
• Smooth muscle
• Cardiac muscle
• Glands
Major divisions:
• Sympathetic →
thoracolumbar outflow
• Parasympathetic →
craniosacral outflow
Both divisions generally use a two-neuron motor pathway
from the CNS to the target organ
Fig. 1.42, 1.47 GAS, 4e.

Somatic vs
Autonomic Motor Pathways
Somatic Motor
• Single motor neuron
• CNS → skeletal muscle
Autonomic Motor
• Two-neuron pathway
• Preganglionic neuron: CNS → autonomic ganglion
• Postganglionic neuron: autonomic ganglion → target organ
• Targets: smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, glands
Autonomic motor pathways
require a synapse in an autonomic ganglion
Fig. 1.42 Clinical Oriented Anatomy, 8e.

Sympathetic System: Thoracolumbar Outflow
Preganglionic neurons
• Cell bodies in the lateral horn (intermediolateral cell column), T1–L2
• Axons exit through ventral roots → enter spinal nerves
• Enter the sympathetic trunk through white rami communicantes
Once in the sympathetic trunk, preganglionic fibers may:
• Synapse at the same level
• Ascend or descend before synapsing
• Pass through without synapsing → splanchnic nerves
Thoracic spinal cord. Courtesy of Univ of Michigan Med School, ©2012; Fig 1.44 GAS, 5e.

White and Gray Rami Communicantes
• White rami: carry preganglionic sympathetic fibers into the sympathetic trunk
• Gray rami: carry postganglionic sympathetic fibers back to the spinal nerve
• White rami: T1–L2 only
• Gray rami: present at all spinal levels
Sympathetic trunk
Gray rami allow sympathetic fibers to reach
the body wall and limbs at all spinal levels

Sympathetic Splanchnic Nerves
Thoracic and Lumbar Splanchnic Nerves
• Carry primarily preganglionic sympathetic fibers
• Fibers pass through the sympathetic trunk without synapsing
• Travel to prevertebral ganglia and autonomic plexuses
Sacral Splanchnic Nerves
• Preganglionic fibers descend in the sympathetic trunk
• Synapse in sacral sympathetic ganglia
• Postganglionic fibers leave as sacral splanchnic nerves
• Contribute to the inferior hypogastric plexus
Do not confuse:
• Sacral splanchnic nerves = sympathetic
• Pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4) = parasympathetic
Fig. 4.136 Splanchnic nerves. GAS, 4e.

Sympathetic Innervation of Abdominal Viscera
Sympathetic Pathway
• Preganglionic fibers pass through the sympathetic trunk without synapsing
• Form thoracic and lumbar splanchnic nerves
• Synapse primarily in prevertebral ganglia
• Postganglionic fibers follow arteries to abdominal viscera
Major Prevertebral Ganglia / Plexuses
• Celiac → primarily foregut
• Superior mesenteric → primarily midgut
• Inferior mesenteric → primarily hindgut
Spinal cord → ventral root → spinal nerve → white ramus
→ sympathetic trunk → thoracic/lumbar splanchnic nerve
→ prevertebral ganglion → periarterial plexus → organ
Fig. 4.136 Splanchnic nerves. GAS, 4e.

Parasympathetic System: Craniosacral Outflow
Preganglionic neurons originate in:
• Brainstem → CN III, VII, IX, X
• Sacral parasympathetic nucleus (S2–S4)
Organization
• Long preganglionic fibers
• Synapse in ganglia near or within target organs
• Short postganglionic fibers → targets
Major Visceral Pathways
• CN III, VII, IX → head and neck structures
• Vagus nerve (CN X) → thoracic viscera, foregut, and midgut
• Preganglionic fibers from S2–S4 form pelvic splanchnic nerves
→ hindgut and pelvic viscera
Fig. 1.47 GAS, 4e.

Parasympathetic Innervation of the Abdominal Viscera
Parasympathetic Pathway
• Vagus nerve (CN X) → foregut and midgut
• Pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4) → hindgut
• Preganglionic fibers extend to the target organ
• Synapse in terminal/intramural ganglia
Functional Effects
• ↑ GI motility
• ↑ GI secretion
Vagus nerve or pelvic splanchnic (S2–S4) nerves →
terminal/intramural ganglia → short postganglionic
fibers → GI effectors
Fig. 1.47 GAS, 4e.

Pelvic Autonomics: Hypogastric Plexuses
Sympathetic
• Abdominal aortic plexus → superior hypogastric plexus
• Superior hypogastric plexus → right and left hypogastric nerves
• Hypogastric nerves → inferior hypogastric plexuses
• Sacral splanchnic nerves contribute to inferior hypogastric plexus
Parasympathetic
• Pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4)
• Contribute to the inferior hypogastric plexus
• Inferior hypogastric plexus contains both sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers
• Distributes to pelvic viscera and hindgut
Fig. 4.136 Splanchnic nerves. GAS, 4e.

Enteric Nervous System
Intrinsic Neural Network of the GI tract
• Myenteric (Auerbach) plexus → primarily regulates motility
• Submucosal (Meissner) plexus → secretion and local blood flow
• Can coordinate GI activity independently
• Modulated by sympathetic and parasympathetic input
Visceral
Fig. 4.139 The enteric system. GAS, 4e.

Autonomic Innervation of the GI Tract
Sympathetic
• Foregut & midgut → thoracic splanchnic nerves
• Hindgut → primarily lumbar splanchnic nerves
• Synapse in prevertebral ganglia
• Postganglionic fibers follow periarterial plexuses
• Generally, ↓ motility and secretion
Parasympathetic
• Foregut & midgut → vagus nerve (CN X)
• Hindgut → pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4)
• Synapse in terminal/intramural ganglia
• Generally, ↑ motility and secretion

Somatic vs Visceral Sensory Pathways
Somatic Sensory (Afferent) Visceral Sensory (Afferent)
• From skin, skeletal muscle, and joints • From viscera and blood vessels
• Carries touch, pain, temperature, and proprioception • Carries distension, chemical changes, and visceral pain
• Cell bodies in dorsal root ganglia (DRG) • Cell bodies in sensory ganglia (DRG, cranial sensory ganglia)
• Fibers enter the spinal cord through posterior roots • Spinal visceral afferents enter through posterior roots
Sensory → CNS: Somatic afferents | Visceral afferents
Motor → Effectors: Somatic → skeletal muscle | Autonomic → viscera
Clinical Anatomy Pearl
• Visceral pain afferents → commonly accompany sympathetic pathways
• Physiologic/reflex afferents → commonly accompany parasympathetic pathways

Terms of Orientation
Spinal Cord
• Anterior = Ventral
• Posterior = Dorsal
• Superior = Rostral
• Inferior = Caudal
Brain
• Anterior = Rostral
• Posterior = Caudal
• Superior = Dorsal
• Inferior = Ventral
Orientation shifts at the cephalic flexure

Central Nervous System Overview
Brain
• Cerebrum
• Brainstem
• Cerebellum
Spinal cord
Fig. 3.1, 3.2 Costanzo, 7e.

Gray Matter vs. White Matter
Gray Matter
• Neuronal cell bodies, dendrites, and
unmyelinated axons
• Site of information processing
• Appears gray in fresh tissue
White Matter
• Myelinated axons (tracts)
• Carries information between regions
• Appears white due to myelin
Organization
• Brain: Gray matter outside, white matter inside
• Spinal Cord: Gray matter inside, white matter outside
Gray matter lesions: focal deficits (e.g., stroke → weakness, aphasia)
White matter lesions: tract conduction deficits (multiple sclerosis →
widespread or dissociated deficits

Neuron
Three Main Parts
• Dendrites → receive input
• Cell body (soma) → integrates signals
• Axon → transmits output
Signal Transmission
• Action potentials begin at the axon hillock
• Axon terminals release neurotransmitters at synapses
Organization
• Tracts = axon bundles in the CNS
• Nerves = axon bundles in the PNS
• Nuclei = neuron cell body clusters in the CNS
• Ganglia = neuron cell body clusters in the PNS
Neuronal loss is largely irreversible
Early reperfusion preserves brain function

Neuroglia (Glial Cells)
Major Functions
• Support and protect neurons
• Form myelin
• Participate in immune defense
CNS Glia
• Astrocytes
• Oligodendrocytes
• Microglia
• Ependymal cells
PNS Glia
• Schwann cells
• Satellite cells
Medical gallery of Blausen Medical 2014. www.Blausen.com

High-Yield Glial Cells
Cell Type Primary Function Clinical Association
Astrocyte Blood-brain barrier, support Astrocytoma; Glioblastoma (GBM)
Oligodendrocyte CNS myelin Multiple sclerosis
Microglia CNS macrophages (immune defense) Neuroinflammation
Ependymal Cell CSF production / circulation Ependymoma
Schwann Cell PNS myelin, axonal regeneration Guillain-Barré, Schwannoma
Satellite Cell Support neurons in ganglia Herpes zoster
Anatomy Pearls Clinical Pearl
• Oligodendrocyte = CNS myelin Optic Nerve ≠ Typical Peripheral Nerve
• Schwann cell = PNS myelin • CNS tract
• One oligodendrocyte → many axons • Myelinated by oligodendrocytes
• One Schwann cell → one axon segment • Optic neuritis is common in MS

Summary
• Nervous system organization includes CNS/PNS and sensory/motor divisions.
• Anterior roots are motor; posterior roots are sensory; spinal nerves and rami are mixed.
• Autonomic motor pathways use preganglionic and postganglionic neurons.
• Sympathetic: thoracolumbar (T1–L2); parasympathetic: craniosacral.
• Sympathetic fibers travel through sympathetic trunks, splanchnic nerves, and
autonomic plexuses.
• Gray matter contains neuronal cell bodies; white matter contains predominantly
myelinated axons.
• Neurons transmit signals; glial cells support, protect, and myelinate neurons.

Overview of the
Nervous System

Meninges and Ventricular System
Aftab Merchant, MBBS, FCPS, MHPE
Professor of Medical Education
Assistant Dean of Anatomical Education
Kirk Kerkorian School of Medicine
University of Nevada Las Vegas

Learning Objectives (2026)
1. Describe the anatomy and organization of the meninges, ventricular system, and
cerebrospinal fluid pathways, and relate their structural relationships to normal central
nervous system protection and function. (CLO 1)
2. Interpret the meninges, ventricular system, and cerebrospinal fluid spaces using cross-
sectional anatomy and medical imaging, and correlate normal imaging anatomy with common
neurological disorders. (CLO 1, CLO 5)
3. Explain the pathophysiology, clinical features, and diagnostic principles of hydrocephalus and
other disorders involving cerebrospinal fluid circulation and the meninges. (CLO 3)

Skull

• +6 auditory ossicles
• Neurocranium: calvaria, cranial base

Skull Sutures

Skull Superior View

Self-Study
Cranial Floor (Fossae Overview)
• Anterior: frontal lobes
• Middle: temporal lobes
• Posterior: cerebellum, brainstem
Credit:KennethSaladin
Fig.7.41Brainanditsrelationshiptothethreecranialfossae
Grant’sDissector,16e.

Cranial Floor
Basilar Skull Fracture
• Fractures involving the skull base
• Commonly involves the temporal bone
Clinical Signs
• Battle sign: postauricular/mastoid ecchymosis
• Hemotympanum: blood behind the tympanic membrane
• Raccoon eyes: periorbital ecchymosis
• CSF leakage: CSF rhinorrhea or otorrhea

Battle Sign and Raccoon Eyes
Battle sign ➔ basilar skull fracture ➔ postauricular/mastoid ecchymosis
Raccoon sign ➔ anterior cranial fossa fracture ➔ periorbital ecchymosis
Image:Piedade.FacialTrauma.
In:TheSportsMedicinePhysician.Springer2019.
Meninges

Meninges
• Dura mater – outermost
• Arachnoid mater – middle
• Pia mater – innermost
Leptomeninges = arachnoid + pia
Fig.8.28,ClinicallyOrientedAnatomy9e.

Dura Mater
• Thick, tough outer meningeal layer
• Cranial dura: periosteal (outer) + meningeal (inner) layers
• Spinal dura: meningeal layer only
• Meningeal layer forms dural partitions
Fig.8.31ADuralpartitions.GAS,5e.

Dural Partitions
• Dural folds that subdivide the cranial cavity
• Falx cerebri: separates cerebral hemispheres
• Tentorium cerebelli: separates cerebrum from cerebellum
• Falx cerebelli: separates cerebellar hemispheres
• Diaphragma sellae: covers pituitary gland in sella turcica
Supratentorial = above the tentorium cerebelli
Infratentorial = below the tentorium cerebelli
Fig.8.32Duralpartitions.
Gray’sAnatomyforStudents,4e.

Dural Innervation
Supratentorial Dura
• Primarily trigeminal nerve (CN V)
• Irritation ➔ referred pain to trigeminal distribution
(forehead, face)
Posterior Fossa Dura
• Primarily upper cervical nerves (C1–3)
• Irritation ➔ referred pain to necck/occiput
Fig.8.34Duralinnervation
Gray’sAnatomyforStudents,4e.

Arachnoid and Pia
Arachnoid Mater
• Middle meningeal layer; avascular
• Does not follow gyri and sulci
• Subarachnoid space contains CSF and cerebral vessels
• Arachnoid granulations → CSF drainage into dural venous sinuses
Pia Mater
• Innermost, delicate vascular membrane
• Adheres closely to brain and spinal cord
• Follows gyri and sulci
Fig.8.35Arrangementofmeningesandspaces.GAS5e.

Meningeal Spaces
Space Type Normal Contents Clinical
Extradural (epidural) Potential None MMA rupture ➔ epidural hematoma
Subdural Potential None Bridging vein tear ➔ subdural hematoma
Subarachnoid Real CSF, vessels Berry aneurysm rupture ➔ SAH
Fig.8.35Arrangementofmeningesandspaces.
Gray’sAnatomyforStudents,5e.

Intracranial Hematomas
Extradural (Epidural) Hematoma
• Middle meningeal artery rupture (pterion fracture)
• Lucid interval ➔ rapid deterioration
• Biconvex lens-shaped hematoma; does not cross sutures
Subdural Hematoma
• Bridging vein tear
• Risk” elderly (brain atrophy) and infants (shaken babies)
• Crescent-shaped hematoma; crosses sutures
Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
• Ruptured berry aneurysm (commonly anterior communicating artery) Fig.8.49Scalpandmeninges
Gray’sAnatomyforStudents,4e.
• Thunderclap headache (“worst headache of my life”), meningeal signs
• CT: blood in basal cisterns/sulci

Epidural (Extradural) Hematoma
• Lens-shaped (biconvex) hematoma
• Limited by sutures (does not cross)
• Displaces brain tissue medially
Subdural Hematoma
• Crescent-shaped hematoma
• Crosses sutures, but not midline falx
• More diffuse, spreads along brain surface
Lens = Epidural
Crescent = Subdural

Herniation Syndromes
↑ Intracranial pressure ➔ displacement of brain tissue across dural partitions
Subfalcine: Cingulate gyrus under falx ➔ACA compression
Central (transtentorial)
• Downward displacement ➔ brainstem compression
Uncal
• ipsilateral CN III compression ➔ dilated pupil;
• cerebral peduncle compression ➔ hemiparesis
Tonsillar
• cerebellar tonsils through foramen magnum ➔ medullary compression
Complications:
Brainstem compression ➔ coma, cardiorespiratory failure, death
CSF & Ventricular System

Ventricular System
• Interconnected CSF-filled cavities
• Lined by ependymal cells
• Four ventricles: two lateral, third, fourth
• Fourth ventricle continues with the central
canal of the spinal cord
Fig.11-1.VentricularSystem.Waxman,30e.

Lateral Ventricles
• C-shaped ventricles in cerebral hemispheres
• Consist of body + 3 horns (anterior, posterior, inferior)
• Communicate with the third ventricle via the
interventricular foramina (of Monro)

Third and Fourth Ventricles
• Third ventricle: between the thalami
• 4th ventricle: between brainstem and cerebellum
• Connected by the cerebral aqueduct
• CSF exits the 4th ventricle into the subarachnoid
space through:
• Two lateral foramina (Luschka)
• One median foramen (Magendie)

Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF)
• Clear, colorless fluid produced primarily by choroid plexus
• Circulates through ventricles ➔ subarachnoid space
• Reabsorbed through arachnoid granulations ➔ dural venous sinuses
• drains into superior sagittal sinus via arachnoid villi
• Functions: buoyancy, protection, and CNS homeostasis
Choroid Plexus
• Vascular tissue covered by modified ependymal cells
• Present in the ventricles
• Main site of CSF production
Lateral ventricles → interventricular foramina → 3rd ventricle → cerebral
aqueduct → 4th ventricle → Luschka/Magendie → subarachnoid space
→ arachnoid granulations → dural venous sinuses

Hydrocephalus
Definition
• Abnormal accumulation of CSF ➔ ventricular dilation ± increased ICP
Causes
• Obstruction of CSF flow ➔ non-communicating (obstructive)
• Impaired CSF absorption ➔ communicating
• CSF overproduction ➔ rare (e.g., choroid plexus papilloma)
Clinical Features
• Headache, nausea/vomiting, papilledema
• Cognitive or neurologic deficits
• Infants: increasing head circumference, bulging fontanelle

Communicating Hydrocephalus
• No obstruction within the ventricular system
• ↓ CSF absorption at arachnoid granulations
• All ventricles enlarge
• Causes: SAH, meningitis
• May cause ↑ ICP

Non-Communicating (Obstructive) Hydrocephalus
• Obstructive within the ventricular system
• Ventricles proximal to the obstruction enlarge
Common Sites of Obstruction
• Interventricular foramen
• Cerebral aqueduct (most common)
• Fourth ventricular outlets
Causes
• Congenital malformations, tumors, cysts, hemorrhage

Mechanical Obstruction
Aqueductal Stenosis, Chiari, Dandy-Walker

Aqueductal Stenosis
• Obstruction of the cerebral aqueduct
• Blocks CSF flow: 3rd → 4th ventricle
• Enlarged lateral and 3rd ventricles
• Normal 4th ventricle
• Congenital or acquired
• Infants: ↑ head circumference, signs of ↑ ICP
• Adults: ↑ ICP, headaches, ↓ consciousness

Chiari II Malformation (Arnold-Chiari Malformation)
• Small/crowded posterior fossa ➔ hindbrain displaced downward
• Crowding impairs CSF flow ➔ noncommunicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus
• Strongly associated with myelomeningocele
• Infants may have feeding difficulty, weak cry, and signs of ↑ ICP
Chiari I
• Cerebellar tonsillar herniation
• Typically presents later
• No myelomeningocele
Chiari II = small posterior fossa + hindbrain herniation + myelomeningocele + hydrocephalus
Chiari I = tonsillar herniation only, no myelomeningocele

Dandy-Walker Malformation (DWM)
• Hypoplasia / agenesis of cerebellar vermis
• ➔ Cystically dilated 4th ventricle; enlarged posterior fossa
• ➔ impaired CSF flow
• ➔ Obstructive hydrocephalus
Clinical Features
• Hydrocephalus (macrocephaly)
• Delayed motor development and ataxia
Dandy-Walker = enlarged posterior fossa
Chiari II = crowded posterior fossa
fetalhealthfoundation.org

Pressure Disorders
Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (pseudotumor Cerebri)
Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH)
Hydrocephalus Ex vacuo (ventriculomegaly due to brain atrophy; not true hydrocephalus)

Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (Pseudotumor Cerebri)
• ↑ ICP with normal ventricular size on imaging
• No mass lesion or hydrocephalus
• Classically occurs in young woman with obesity
• Headache, papilledema, transient visual loss
• Pulsatile tinnitus (key diagnostic clue)
• CN VI palsy may cause diplopia
• LP: ↑ opening pressure with normal CSF composition
• Tx: weight loss + acetazolamide
• Often associated with transverse venous narrowing
Some casesof pseudotumorcerebrimay resultfrom
narrowing(red)of cerebraldrainingveins(blue).
Image: neurosurgery.weillcornell.org

Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH)
• Usually occurs in older adults
• Ventriculomegaly out of proportion to cortical atrophy
Classic Triad
• Urinary incontinence; gait disturbance; dementia
• CSF opening pressure may be normal when measured
• Tx: ventriculoperitoneal shunt
Traditional Explanation
• Thought to involve impaired CSF absorption
➔ ventricular enlargement compresses corona radiata
NPH = “wet, wobbly, wacky”
Non-contrastCTdemonstratesenlargedlateralventricles(whitearrows)
Gait disturbance typically occurs first withoutsignificantcerebralatrophy.(CourtesyofReginaldDusing,MD.)

Hydrocephalus Ex Vacuo
• Ventricular enlargement due to loss of brain tissue
• Compensatory enlargement of ventricles and sulci
• Not due to CSF obstruction or impaired absorption
• ICP is normal
• Seen in neurodegeneration (Alzheimer), stroke, or
other causes of brain atrophy
• Despite the name, not true hydrocephalus
NPH: ventriculomegaly + clinical triad
Ex vacuo: ventriculomegaly + brain atrophy
Kim.PsychiatryInvestig.2021

Summary
• Meninges: dura → arachnoid → pia
• Spaces: epidural/subdural = potential; subarachnoid = CSF + vessels
• Hemorrhage: epidural = MMA; subdural = bridging veins; SAH = subarachnoid
• ↑ ICP → brain herniation across dural partitions
• CSF: choroid plexus → ventricles → subarachnoid space → venous sinuses
• Hydrocephalus: communicating = ↓ absorption; obstructive = blocked flow
• Key disorders have characteristic ventricular and imaging patterns
